  • RPNHead scans the pyramid for objectness and turns raw anchors into the proposals the second stage refines.
  • StandardRoIHead samples those proposals, pools their features, and delegates classification, box refinement and (optionally) masking to sub-heads.
  • FPN fuses the stage outputs of ResNet into a multi-scale pyramid — the same slot where a Swin Transformer backbone or a PAFPN variant plugs in.
  • RTMDet shows the single-stage alternative in the same panel: one dense head reading a PAFPN-fed pyramid, no proposal step at all.

The Detail Diagram: Heads, Hooks and Data

Figure 2 — the full map: detector families on the left, the dense-head and RoI-head hierarchies in the middle, backbones and task modules at the bottom, and the data-to-metric loop closing on the right.

The detail view makes the two inheritance axes obvious. Down the left side, detectors specialize: BaseDetector spawns TwoStageDetector, SingleStageDetector and a shared DetectionTransformer for query-based models. Two-stage then splits into FasterRCNN, MaskRCNN and CascadeRCNN, while the single-stage line leads to RTMDet and the transformer line to DETR.

Down the middle run the heads. Dense heads all descend from BaseDenseHead; its anchor-aware child AnchorHead is the parent of RPNHead, RetinaHead and ATSSHead, whose descendant RTMDetHead powers the real-time family. Anchors themselves are laid out by AnchorGenerator, a task module that heads receive as a configurable component rather than hardcode. On the RoI side, BaseRoIHead begets StandardRoIHead and CascadeRoIHead; the former delegates box work to BBoxHead and its two-shared-FC child Shared2FCBBoxHead, and masks to FCNMaskHead. A query-based model instead leans on DETRHead, which turns decoder embeddings into boxes with no anchors anywhere.

The right edge of the diagram is the plumbing that makes training reproducible. CocoDataset yields per-image records wrapped in DetDataSample; DetDataPreprocessor normalizes, pads and stacks them into batches before the model ever sees a tensor; predictions ride back inside the same container to DetVisualizationHook and to CocoMetric, which computes COCO-style mAP.

The bottom edge is where the pixels get read. Two-stage recipes mostly sit on ResNet, whose four stage outputs feed FPN into five pyramid levels. RTMDet swaps in CSPNeXt, a cross-stage partial backbone with depthwise-friendly blocks, and drains it through PAFPN, which adds a bottom-up path so low-level localization detail survives the trip to the head. Because both sides of that exchange are just registry keys, changing the feature extractor for a whole family of models is a two-line config edit — the sort of experiment that used to require forking the entire training script.

From Install to Your First Model

The blessed route is via OpenMMLab’s own package manager:

pip install -U openmim
mim install "mmcv>=2.0.0"
mim install "mmdet>=3.0.0"

With that in place, inference is three lines — no config file hunting required:

from mmdet.apis import DetInferencer

model = DetInferencer("rtmdet_s_8xb32-300e_coco")
result = model("demo/demo.jpg", out_dir="outputs")

DetInferencer resolves the config name against the OpenMMLab model zoo, downloads weights on first use, and handles the preprocessing and result drawing internally. Under the hood this is the same machinery you saw in Figure 1: the string is a config path, the config names every module, and the registry instantiates the whole stack from backbone to metric.

Training follows the same declarative logic. From a repository clone:

python tools/train.py configs/rtmdet/rtmdet_s_8xb32-300e_coco.py
python tools/test.py  configs/rtmdet/rtmdet_s_8xb32-300e_coco.py \
    checkpoints/rtmdet_s_8xb32-300e_coco.pth

The two commands differ only in which forward mode the runner drives. If you want a Faster R-CNN baseline instead, swap the config path — nothing else changes, because TwoStageDetector and its children already exist behind the registry.

The config you just passed around is itself an exercise in inheritance. It opens with _base_ = '../_base_/schedules/schedule_1x.py'-style pointers that pull in a standard schedule, a standard dataset wrapper and standard runtime defaults, then overrides only what makes RTMDet special: the head, the loss weights, the augmentation schedule. When you later wonder why your model trains with a particular learning-rate rule you never typed, the answer is almost always three _base_ hops up the chain. Custom datasets usually mean reusing CocoDataset with a different annotation file and overriding classes in your config — genuinely most of the work for a standard detection project, with the framework absorbing the rest.

How Training Really Runs

Nothing in your config is a Python training loop — MMEngine supplies one. Its runner reads the config, builds the model, the data loading stack and the optimizer, then walks epochs through train and validation loops. Every epoch, the runner pulls batches from the dataloader; the data loading stack — dataset, transforms, and the detector’s data preprocessor — has already turned raw COCO dictionaries into DetDataSample objects with normalized, padded tensors. The model’s loss method consumes those batches and returns a dict of named losses; the runner back-propagates the sum and lets the optimizer step.

The hook system is what makes this extensible. Checkpointing, logging, learning-rate scheduling and the visualization hook all register into a timeline that fires before and after epochs, iterations and validation passes. You can write a hook in ten lines, register it in your config, and it sits next to the built-ins — that is exactly how the semi-supervised and mean-teacher variants in the repo extend training without forking the loop.

Evaluation closes the loop with the same containers. After each validation pass, the tester collects DetDataSample predictions, hands them to CocoMetric together with the ground truth kept in the dataset, and reports mAP per class. Because predictions and annotations travel in the same structure end to end, adding a new metric or dataset rarely touches model code — which is precisely the separation the config-driven design was built to buy you.

Scaling follows the same pattern. The batch size and worker count are baked into config ids themselves — 8xb32 literally means eight GPUs at batch 32 — and switching to multi-machine training is a launcher flag on the tools, not a code change. Mixed precision, gradient accumulation and per-parameter optimizer groups are all schedule-level settings that live beside the model definition, which is why reproducing a paper number is usually a matter of picking the right config id rather than reverse-engineering an args namespace.

Honest Limits

The design has costs, and they are worth naming before you build on it. Config sprawl is the first: because models are assembled declaratively, a Mask R-CNN recipe inherits from a generic two-stage base that inherits from a dataset definition, and by the time you have followed four _base_ hops you are reading five files to answer one question. Second, the 2.x-to-3.x transition reorganized nearly every import path and config id; tutorials from 2021 are actively misleading today, and the mmdet.apis surface shrank to the inferencer you saw above. Third, MMCV version pinning is real friction — matching CUDA, PyTorch and mmcv wheels is the most common install failure, and it bites hardest on Windows.

Scope is also narrower than the name suggests. MMDetection is a detection toolbox, not a general vision platform: no classification, no diffusion, no LLM-adjacent tooling, and tracking lives in a separate repository. If you want a single-file training script you can fork in an afternoon, YOLOv5 or its Ultralytics successors are friendlier; if you want research-grade reference implementations with a different config philosophy, Detectron2 remains the rival worth reading next to this codebase. But for breadth of detectors, reproducibility of published numbers, and a registry/config architecture that scales across hundreds of models, MMDetection is still the reference — and now you know where its seams are.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the MMDetection 3.x source tree: detectors, heads, backbones, hooks and metrics, with two architecture diagrams and line-verified code anchors.

entry.title: PyTorch Geometric: A Source Tour of the Graph Neural Network Library

link.title: PyTorch Geometric: A Source Tour of the Graph Neural Network Library

entry.content:
Graph neural networks occupy a peculiar spot in deep learning research: everyone agrees they matter, yet the mechanics of a GNN layer feel far more opaque than those of a convolution or a transformer block. Images come with a fixed grid and a battle-tested toolkit; graphs bring arbitrary topology, ragged neighborhoods, and batches that are not tensors at all. PyTorch Geometric — usually abbreviated PyG — is the library that made this manageable on PyTorch, and it is now the de facto standard for GNN work in the PyTorch ecosystem, powering everything from citation-network tutorials to drug-discovery and recommender systems in production.

The library deserves a source tour for the same reason PyTorch itself does: its most valuable ideas are not in the README but in the way a handful of abstractions interlock. PyG is built around four load-bearing pillars. First, a Data object that represents one graph as plain tensors plus an edge_index matrix. Second, a data loading flow that can either stack whole graphs into mega-batches or sample subgraphs out of graphs far too large to fit in memory. Third, a message-passing engine that reduces every published GNN layer — GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT and hundreds more — to a small set of overridable functions. Fourth, scatter-based aggregation kernels that do the heavy lifting whenever many edges must be reduced onto the same node.

Understanding how these pillars connect explains most of what makes PyG feel the way it does in daily use: why handing a DataLoader a list of Data objects yields a Batch, why sampling loaders return ever-growing node sets per hop, and why a custom GNN layer is often under forty lines of code. This post walks the actual source tree of the repository, with diagrams and line-level links, so you can use it as a map the next time a training loop misbehaves or a paper’s equation needs to become a layer.

The five load-bearing regions of PyG: the Data layer, the loading and sampling flow, the message-passing family, scatter-based aggregation and pooling, and the ready-made GNN models built on top of all four.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at Dataset, L30, the abstract base that defines the download/process/len/getitem protocol every PyG dataset implements. The in-memory flavor at InMemoryDataset, L32 caches a whole corpus as a single collated tensor store.
  • One graph is one Data, L472 instance: x for node features, edge_index for connectivity in COO format, plus arbitrary extra tensors.
  • The classic DataLoader, L52 subclasses torch.utils.data.DataLoader and swaps the collation function so that a list of graphs becomes one parallel Batch object.
  • When a single graph is too big to batch, NeighborLoader, L10 delegates to a sampling engine descended from BaseSampler, L932 and returns subgraph-shaped Data objects instead.
  • Every convolution in the library descends from MessagePassing, L39. Concrete layers such as GCNConv, L116, SAGEConv, L13 and GATConv, L35 differ only in how they compute and reduce messages.
  • The reduction itself flows through Aggregation, L10, while graph-level classification tasks use readouts like global_mean_pool, L37.
  • Finally, batteries-included classifiers like the GCN model, L389 stack conv layers behind a uniform training interface, so a baseline is one constructor call away.

From Install to Your First Model

PyG installs like any other PyTorch extension: pip install torch_geometric works out of the box with recent PyTorch versions, and the optional accelerators torch_scatter, torch_sparse, torch_cluster and torch_spline_conv only buy you speed and a few extra algorithms — the pure-PyTorch core works without a compiler.

The canonical hello world trains a two-layer GCN on Cora, a citation graph with about 2,700 paper nodes and seven classes. The dataset side is one line, because Planetoid, L11 subclasses InMemoryDataset and downloads, processes and caches everything on first use:

from torch_geometric.datasets import Planetoid
dataset = Planetoid(root="/tmp/Cora", name="Cora")
data = dataset[0]           # one big Data object, train/val/test masks included

The model side shows why the template BasicGNN classes exist:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch_geometric.nn import GCN

model = GCN(dataset.num_features, 16, dataset.num_classes, num_layers=2)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01, weight_decay=5e-4)

for epoch in range(200):
    out = model(data.x, data.edge_index)   # logits for every node
    loss = F.cross_entropy(out[data.train_mask], data.y[data.train_mask])
    optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()

That loop is full-batch training: the whole graph goes through the network each step, and the GCN model from basic_gnn.py handles the conv stack, dropout and classification head for you. If you would rather assemble layers yourself, the explicit equivalent uses GCNConv, L116 directly — GCNConv(in, out) twice with F.relu between them — and behaves identically. One small but telling detail: calling seed_everything, L7 before the loop reseeds Python, NumPy and PyTorch in one shot — handy, because Cora runs are annoyingly unstable otherwise.

The Data Layer: Graphs as Tensors with Topology

The entire input side of PyG rests on Data, L472. Its central convention is edge_index: an int64 tensor of shape [2, num_edges] holding source and destination node indices. Nothing else about a graph is mandatory: node labels are just another tensor, and heterogeneous graphs extend the same idea with string-qualified node and edge types — the typing module formalizes those as NodeType and EdgeType aliases. This “dictionary of tensors” design is why PyG composes so cleanly with PyTorch autograd: gradients flow through x and edge weights like through any tensor operation.

Datasets wrap collections of Data objects. The split between Dataset, L30 and InMemoryDataset, L32 is a deliberate memory trade: the former keeps a Python list and loads items lazily from disk, while the latter calls collate() once and stores the entire corpus as concatenated tensors with index pointers — precisely how Planetoid and most benchmark suites ship. When you then iterate a loader, collate, L37 performs the trick that makes batching graphs possible at all: node and edge tensors are concatenated along dimension zero, and a batch vector records which graph each node came from. The result, Batch, L57, is itself a Data subclass, so downstream code never needs a special case — a batch of 32 graphs is just one disconnected graph with 32 components.

Transforms plug into this layer the same way torchvision transforms plug into images. Anything implementing BaseTransform, L6 can be attached to a dataset, and Compose, L7 chains several together; NormalizeFeatures, L9 is the one every Cora tutorial uses. Because transforms run inside the dataset, preprocessing happens once at load time instead of per epoch.

Inside the Message-Passing Chain

If you read only one file in PyG, make it message_passing.py. The insight at MessagePassing, L39 is that virtually every GNN layer from the literature fits the same three-step template: compute a message per edge from the endpoint features, aggregate messages per destination node with a permutation-invariant reduction, and update node embeddings with the aggregated result. The base class turns that template into a dispatch loop — propagate, L421 gathers endpoint features, invokes message, L565, then routes the result into aggregate, L577 or, when a fused scatter path is available, straight into message_and_aggregate, L598.

The concrete layers show how little code the template actually needs. GCNConv implements the Kipf-Welling normalization by dividing messages by the square root of endpoint degrees — which it obtains from degree, L9 — and caches the normalized edge weights when the topology is static. SAGEConv concatenates the destination node’s own features with the mean of its neighbors’ messages, exactly the GraphSAGE recipe. GATConv scores each edge with a learned attention coefficient, normalizes those scores with the per-neighbor softmax from softmax, L12, and uses them to weight the aggregation — meaning attention itself is just another differentiable message weighting. All three funnel their reductions through the same scatter kernel at scatter, L14, which dispatches to whichever compiled backend is installed.

The detail view: how Data objects flow through collate and the loaders, how the sampler machinery sits behind NeighborLoader, and how every conv layer leans on the scatter, softmax and degree kernels before handing pooled readouts to the model templates.

The detail diagram above is the map worth keeping open while debugging. It makes two things visually obvious. First, the data loading flow is a funnel — Dataset transforms feed Data, collate feeds Batch, and both the vanilla DataLoader and the sampling loaders sit in front of the conv layers, so shape errors almost always originate left of the model. Second, aggregation is a genuinely separate subsystem: MessagePassing has a default reduction, but any layer accepts a custom Aggregation, L10 module, and simple ones like MeanAggregation, L25 and SumAggregation, L12 are two-liners worth copying when you experiment.

Loading and Sampling at Scale

Full-batch training dies the moment your graph has millions of nodes, so PyG’s answer is mini-batching by neighborhood. The vanilla DataLoader, L52 batches multiple graphs; NeighborLoader, L10 batches parts of one graph. Under the hood it asks the sampler hierarchy — BaseSampler, L932 with the concrete NeighborSampler, L40 — to walk num_neighbors random in-edges per node per hop, then materializes the induced subgraph as a fresh Data object. What you receive in the training loop is the same tensor interface as before, just with progressively larger node sets per layer — the subgraph’s “frontier”.

This shape is worth internalizing because it explains GraphSAGE’s original claim to fame: with two hops of fifteen-and-ten neighbors, a node’s representation depends on a bounded, size-independent slice of the graph, so memory per batch stays constant no matter how big the full adjacency matrix is. The cost is the classic trade-off — sampled training is unbiased only in expectation, and deep stacks with many hops suffer the “neighborhood explosion” where a single seed node drags in thousands of ancestors. Practical guidance falls out of the source structure: keep hops shallow, shrink num_neighbors as depth grows, and reach for the sampling loaders only when the full graph genuinely will not fit — the HuggingFace Datasets library plays a complementary role when your node features, not the graph itself, are the memory hog.

Aggregation and the Scatter Kernel

Every reduce-with-respect-to-index operation in PyG bottoms out at scatter, L14: given values and an index vector, add/mean/max them into slots. This is the GNN analog of matrix multiplication for transformers — the primitive whose efficiency decides the whole library’s throughput. Graph-level tasks add one more consumer: global_mean_pool, L37 runs the same scatter over the batch vector to produce one embedding per graph, which is what turns node-level architectures into graph classifiers, much like the pooled features from scikit-learn reducers.

The Aggregation base class turns that primitive into a first-class extension point. Subclasses implement one reduce call; utilities for multi-head combinations, sorting-based pooling and attention-weighted aggregation all build on it. When a paper proposes a new reduction — power means, soft maximum, anything — the PyG-native way to try it is a small Aggregation subclass rather than a forked conv layer, and the message-passing chain will pick it up through the standard aggr argument.

Honest Limits

Sampling is unbiased in theory and subtly biased in practice. Neighbor sampling’s variance shows up as degraded accuracy on tasks sensitive to high-degree nodes, and several papers report noticeable gaps between full-batch and sampled training on the same model; the library gives you the knobs (num_neighbors, disjoint vs. non-disjoint modes) but not a magic equalizer. The neighborhood explosion also inverts on very dense graphs, where “sample ten neighbors per hop” still yields enormous frontiers.

Heterogeneous graphs work but demand care. The HeteroData variant is genuinely well designed, yet real-world heterogeneous workflows involve a combinatorial spread of edge types, per-type sampling budgets and the notorious to_heterogeneous/to_homogeneous conversions whose failure modes are shape errors deep inside the message-passing chain. Expect to spend a day on schema design before the first epoch runs.

Finally, the dependency surface has sharp edges worth knowing before deployment. The optional acceleration libraries pin specific PyTorch and CUDA combinations, and performance-oriented code paths (fused scatter in particular) differ measurably between setups. Convolutions also evolve faster than tutorials: APIs like the pooling helpers moved across modules over the library’s history — the nn/glob.py path you will still find in old Stack Overflow answers is now a deprecation shim over the real implementation in nn/pool/glob.py. Pin your version, read the changelog on upgrade, and this library’s source will repay the read many times over.

entry.title: SAM 2 Source Tour: How Streaming Memory Powers Promptable Video Segmentation

link.title: SAM 2 Source Tour: How Streaming Memory Powers Promptable Video Segmentation

entry.content:
Segment Anything Model 2, released by Meta’s FAIR lab as the facebookresearch/sam2 repository, is the successor to the original Segment Anything model, and its most important idea is unification: one promptable segmentation model handles both still images and video. You give it clicks, bounding boxes, or a rough mask; it returns high-quality object masks. On images that is a single forward pass. On video, the model treats every frame as a new observation of the same object and tracks the mask forward and backward through the clip, so annotating one object once propagates through the whole sequence. That single design decision is why SAM 2 became the default tool for fast visual annotation and why its demo drew so much attention when it landed.

What makes the source worth reading is the streaming memory architecture under the hood. Most video segmentation systems of its generation leaned on optical flow between frames or on full-graph optimization after the fact. SAM 2 does neither: as it processes frames one at a time, it stores compact spatial memories of what it has already seen — the predicted mask, downsampled and fused with backbone features — and conditions each new frame on that memory bank through cross-attention. There is no second pass over past frames, no expensive temporal smoothing stage, and still the masks stay temporally consistent. Understanding how that loop is wired means reading sam2/modeling/sam2_base.py and the modules it coordinates, which is exactly what this tour does.

To make the structure concrete, we generated two architecture diagrams directly from the repository tree — a compact overview and a detail view that goes down to individual methods. Below we walk the overview left to right, then zoom in, then run the model from a fresh install, and finish with an honest look at the failure modes you will hit in production use.

SAM 2 at a glance: three entry points funnel into SAM2Base, which coordinates the Hiera vision stack, the promptable SAM heads, and the memory modules that carry masks across frames.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at build_sam2, L71, a Hydra-driven factory that composes a model config, instantiates the module tree, and loads the checkpoint. Its sibling build_sam2_video_predictor, L100 builds the same weights but swaps in the video predictor class.
  • On the user side, SAM2ImagePredictor, L20 is the image facade: set_image, L86 embeds the picture once so subsequent prompts are cheap, and predict, L237 turns clicks or boxes into masks. For prompt-free operation, SAM2AutomaticMaskGenerator, L36 grids the image with point prompts and post-processes the result.
  • For video, SAM2VideoPredictor, L19 manages an inference_state dict: init_state, L42 loads and resizes the frames, add_new_points_or_box, L161 registers a prompt on any frame, and propagate_in_video, L546 streams masks through the whole clip.
  • Both predictors delegate to SAM2Base, L22, the real engine. Its per-frame method track_step, L814 is the beating heart of the propagation chain — everything else in the diagram exists to serve it.
  • The vision side is ImageEncoder, L14, which wraps the Hiera, L169 hierarchical ViT trunk and an FPN neck to emit multi-scale feature maps.
  • The promptable heads are PromptEncoder, L17, which embeds clicks, boxes, and masks into sparse and dense tokens, and MaskDecoder, L15, which runs TwoWayTransformer, L19 bidirectional attention before upsampling to mask logits.
  • The memory side is what distinguishes SAM 2 from its predecessor: MemoryEncoder, L138 writes new memories after each frame, and MemoryAttention, L102 conditions current features on everything remembered so far.

What the Detail Diagram Adds

The overview hides the mechanics inside SAM2Base’s one-frame cycle, so the second diagram expands the same repository into thirty-plus nodes grouped by responsibility — assembly, streaming core, SAM heads, vision backbone, memory stack, and support utilities. It is worth a slow scroll before reading the next sections.

The detail view adds per-method nodes: track_step orchestrates memory selection, head decoding, and memory writing for every frame of the propagation chain.

Three clusters deserve attention. First, the streaming core: track_step calls _prepare_memory_conditioned_features to gather memory, _forward_sam_heads to decode masks, and _encode_new_memory to write new memory — a read-decode-write loop per frame. Second, the heads: the mask decoder’s predict_masks path runs the two-way transformer whose cross-attention blocks use RoPEAttention with rotary position embeddings, a detail borrowed from modern LLMs. Third, support: load_video_frames spins up an AsyncVideoFrameLoader that prefetches frames on a background thread so decoding latency hides behind GPU compute, and fill_holes_in_mask_scores cleans disconnected components out of predicted masks.

From Install to Your First Model

SAM 2 targets Python 3.10+ and PyTorch 2.3.1 or newer. From a clone of the repository, an editable install pulls in the handful of dependencies (no CUDA extension compilation is required for inference; building one is optional for training speed):

git clone https://github.com/facebookresearch/sam2.git
cd sam2
pip install -e .

Checkpoints live in the repo’s release and on the Hugging Face hub, where the model identifiers map to config-plus-weight pairs — facebook/sam2.1-hiera-large being the highest-quality variant, with tiny, small, and base-plus siblings trading accuracy for speed. The simplest image workflow skips explicit config handling entirely via from_pretrained:

from sam2.sam2_image_predictor import SAM2ImagePredictor

predictor = SAM2ImagePredictor.from_pretrained("facebook/sam2.1-hiera-large")
predictor.set_image(image)  # np.ndarray (H, W, 3) RGB or PIL image
masks, scores, logits = predictor.predict(
    point_coords=[[600, 400]], point_labels=[1]
)

predict is cheap after set_image because the expensive embedding is computed once and cached; you can add negative clicks with label 0 iteratively until the mask is right. The video workflow mirrors the diagram’s state machine:

from sam2.build_sam import build_sam2_video_predictor

predictor = build_sam2_video_predictor(
    "configs/sam2.1/sam2.1_hiera_l.yaml",
    "checkpoints/sam2.1_hiera_large.pt",
)
state = predictor.init_state("videos/your_clip.mp4")
predictor.add_new_points_or_box(
    state, obj_id=1, points=[[600, 400]], labels=[1]
)
for frame_idx, obj_ids, masks in predictor.propagate_in_video(state):
    pass  # masks per object per frame, streamed as the loop advances

Two practical notes. You can jump to any frame and add new prompts mid-propagation; the model re-runs affected frames rather than everything. And each object gets its own obj_id, so multi-object tracking is a first-class API — though cost grows with object count, as we will see below.

Inside the Streaming Memory Loop

The design question at the core of SAM 2 is: what should a frame know about the past? The answer is a bounded memory bank per object. When SAM2Base, L22 processes frame t, its _prepare_memory_conditioned_features path first asks select_closest_cond_frames (from sam2/modeling/sam2_utils.py) which past frames are worth attending to: every frame where the user prompted (conditioning frames), plus a sliding window of recent frames. Those stored memories — spatial feature maps fused with downsampled predicted masks, plus a single-vector object pointer per memory — are concatenated and fed to the memory cross-attention.

The decoder side then runs as in image segmentation, but with one twist: because memory can make the single best mask ambiguous, the model applies a stability-based fallback, re-picking among multiple mask hypotheses when IoU confidence is low. This dynamic_multimask_via_stability behavior is toggled on by the builder’s default override arguments you saw referenced near build_sam2. After the mask is chosen, _encode_new_memory pushes the frame’s features and the predicted mask through the memory encoder, and the loop advances by one frame. Nothing about the past is recomputed — the propagation chain is strictly O(frames) once prompts are placed.

This is also why the architecture is genuinely streaming: future frames never need to exist when processing frame t, which is what enables the interactive loop of the demo, where you scrub backward, re-prompt, and let only the affected span re-propagate.

Where SAM 2 Fits in the Ecosystem

If you have followed our earlier tours, the lineage is easy to place. The original Segment Anything established the promptable-mask paradigm and the SA-1B dataset, but treated video by per-frame segmentation with no persistence. SAM 2 keeps the data-engine mindset and adds the memory loop, achieving better accuracy with roughly one-sixth the interactive annotations in their ablations. The Hiera backbone itself descends from the MAE-style pretraining line, and if you want to experiment with alternative trunks, the image-encoder wrapper is a thin, clean seam to modify. For classical detection and instance segmentation baselines, Detectron2 remains the reference toolkit, and SAM 2 outputs can be dropped next to its box and mask heads for comparison studies. All of this stands on PyTorch, and the codebase is a pleasant specimen of a research repo: plain nn.Modules, a single Hydra config tree per model variant, and no metaclass magic.

Honest Limits

  • Confusable objects. Tracking relies on appearance plus motion consistency, not identity reasoning. Two visually similar objects crossing paths can swap masks mid-video; the classic failure demo is occlusion followed by re-emergence in a slightly different pose.
  • Memory costs scale with objects and video length. Each object holds its own memory bank on GPU, and long clips accumulate per-frame outputs in inference_state. For long videos with many objects, memory pressure is real; the code offers a vos_optimized build with torch.compile, but the fundamental scaling remains.
  • No semantics. Masks are class-agnostic. SAM 2 will happily segment a shadow or a reflection if prompted; attaching labels, relationships, or filtering by category is your job.
  • Prompt sensitivity in degenerate scenes. Extremely small objects, heavy motion blur, or duplicated textures can yield unstable masks in the first frames, and errors early in the propagation chain persist until you intervene with a corrective prompt.
  • Fixed input resolution. Images are resized to 1024 on the long side by the internal transforms, and video frames to a configured shorter-side size, so sub-pixel boundary fidelity on tiny structures has a ceiling.
  • Checkpoint and license logistics. Weights are released under their own model license (Apache 2.0 for code) and need to be downloaded separately or pulled from the hub — worth automating for reproducible environments.

None of these are disqualifying — they are the edges of a design that chose streaming speed and interactivity over exhaustive global optimization. Reading the source makes those trade-offs explicit, and once you can trace a click through prompt encoding, two-way attention, memory write, and cross-frame readback, SAM 2 stops being a black box and becomes a component you can confidently wire into larger vision systems.

entry.title: scikit-learn Source Tour: The Estimator Contract Behind a Decade of Machine Learning

link.title: scikit-learn Source Tour: The Estimator Contract Behind a Decade of Machine Learning

entry.content:
If you have trained a classifier in Python in the last decade, chances are you did it through scikit-learn. Born as a Google Summer of Code project in 2007 and shepherded since by a famously careful maintainer team, the library sits on NumPy and SciPy and turned machine learning into something you could do in an afternoon: import an estimator, call fit, call predict, move on. What makes it remarkable is not the mathematics alone — logistic regression and k-means are old ideas — but the discipline of its interface. Thousands of estimators, written by hundreds of contributors over many years, all behave the same way. That uniformity is engineered, and the blueprints are public.

That is why the source is worth reading even if you never plan to contribute. scikit-learn is one of the cleanest long-running case studies in API design: a single base class defines the contract, one validation layer guards every entry point, and compiled Cython kernels sit under the hottest loops so the friendly Python surface does not pay a performance tax. Deep learning frameworks get more attention, but the estimator pattern pioneered here quietly shaped how the whole Python ecosystem thinks about models — and how later projects, from PyTorch to Transformers, designed their own training and configuration surfaces.

This tour walks the repository through two diagrams: a compact overview of how the major subsystems relate, and a detail view that follows one path from the Python API all the way down to the Cython metal. Along the way we will read the estimator contract, see how estimator chaining works, descend into the tree-building kernels, and finish with the model selection machinery and an honest look at where the library stops.

The overview map: one estimator contract at the core, a shared validation layer, and the model, selection, and scoring subsystems hanging off it.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Every story starts at BaseEstimator, L165, the shared ancestor that gives all estimators introspectable hyperparameters through get_params and set_params, plus the clone capability everything else depends on.
  • clone, L46 copies an estimator’s configuration but never its learned state, which is the quiet reason cross-validation results in scikit-learn can be trusted.
  • check_array, L729 is the bouncer at the door: raw lists, DataFrames, and ragged arrays all pass through here before any model math happens, with check_X_y, L1180 doing the paired check for labeled data.
  • TransformerMixin, L875 adds the fit/transform pairing — and its fit_transform at L913 is the hook that makes chaining transformers together cheap.
  • On the model side, RandomForestClassifier, L1262 shows the ensemble pattern: many small trees, each built by a Cython kernel, dispatched through Parallel, L41.
  • GridSearchCV, L1344 is the flagship meta-estimator: it sweeps a parameter grid, clones a fresh estimator for every combination, and scores each on cross-validation folds.
  • Finally, accuracy_score, L357 and its siblings form the scoring layer every search and every evaluation bottoms out in.

From Install to Your First Model

Nothing about scikit-learn is exotic to install — it is pure wheels on every mainstream platform, with NumPy, SciPy, and joblib as the only hard friends. The famous five lines still work:

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(accuracy_score(y_te, clf.predict(X_te)))

Each of those lines is a doorway into the source. load_iris returns a small bundled dataset — no download, no network, which is why tutorials love it. train_test_split looks trivial but funnels through the same validation utilities as everything else, deriving its shuffle seed from your random_state. The fit call is where the estimator contract takes over: input validation, a hand-off to compiled builders, and a fitted object returned as self. predict is deliberately boring — array validation again, then a vectorized pass over the learned structure.

Two source landmarks round out the layer. The top-level sklearn/__init__.py re-exports the public surface by hand. And for exploring rather than consuming, all_estimators in sklearn/utils/discovery.py, L22 enumerates every estimator class in the package, filterable by kind.

The fit/transform Contract and Estimator Chaining

Open sklearn/base.py and you find the whole philosophy in one file. BaseEstimator does not know anything about learning; it knows about configuration. Its get_params at L248 inspects the estimator’s own __init__ signature and returns exactly the keyword arguments it was born with. This one decision — hyperparameters only in the constructor, data only in fit — is what makes every downstream tool possible: you can serialize, compare, and rebuild any estimator from its parameter dictionary, with no hidden state.

clone at L46 is the enforcement arm of that decision. It takes an estimator, pulls its params, and constructs a brand-new unfitted twin, raising an error if any constructor default was tampered with. Cross-validation and grid search lean on this constantly: nothing ever reuses a fitted model across folds, so there is no leakage by construction. Mixins then layer on capabilities: ClassifierMixin, L561 contributes a score method and tags, RegressorMixin, L631 and ClusterMixin, L719 do the same for their families, and is_classifier at L1245 is the runtime test the rest of the library uses to branch on estimator kind.

The transformer half of the contract is fit returning self and transform turning data into data. TransformerMixin composes them into fit_transform, and since fit hands back the object itself, calls chain naturally: scaler.fit(X).transform(X) reads like a sentence. This contract is what estimator chaining is built on — scikit-learn ships a helper that stitches a list of transformers to a final estimator into one composite object, and that helper contains no magic beyond calling fit_transform down the line and fit at the end. The composition exists so cross-validation treats the entire chain as one unit: the scaler learns its statistics inside each fold, never from held-out data. Doing it by hand — fit the scaler on the training fold, transform both folds, fit the model — gives exactly the same semantics.

The newest contract extension is metadata routing, and its layout teaches how the project evolves without breaking old imports. BaseEstimator inherits _MetadataRequester from sklearn/utils/_metadata_requests.py, L1665, where MetadataRequest, L633 records which keywords an estimator is willing to receive and MetadataRouter, L980 lets meta-estimators declare where those keywords should flow. The file you might import by name, sklearn/utils/metadata_routing.py, is now a thin re-export shim — a live example of the project treating its import surface as a public promise.

Under the Hood: Cython Kernels and Parallel Dispatch

The detail view: Python estimators on top, the validation and parallelism utilities in the middle, and the Cython kernels doing the heavy lifting underneath.

The detail diagram above is really a story about two languages. Python owns the parts where flexibility matters — API, validation, orchestration — and Cython owns the parts where the inner loop would otherwise drown in interpreter overhead. The cleanest example is a single decision tree. DecisionTreeClassifier in sklearn/tree/_classes.py is a friendly Python class, but its fit immediately hands control to sklearn/tree/_tree.pyx, a depth-first builder that recurses over nodes in compiled code. Each node asks sklearn/tree/_splitter.pyx to hunt for the best feature and threshold, and the splitter scores every candidate using the Gini and entropy kernels in sklearn/tree/_criterion.pyx. None of that allocates a Python object per candidate.

The same pattern repeats across the library once you know to look for it. K-means is a Python orchestrator in sklearn/cluster/_kmeans.py wrapped around a Lloyd iteration kernel in sklearn/cluster/_k_means_lloyd.pyx, which does the assignment and center-update passes on contiguous arrays. The penalized linear models use a coordinate-descent inner loop in sklearn/linear_model/_cd_fast.pyx, and the gradient boosting family keeps its regression-tree kernels in sklearn/ensemble/_gradient_boosting.pyx. The names end in .pyx, and finding them in the tree is the fastest way to locate the true hot spots of any subsystem.

Parallelism gets the same treatment. sklearn/utils/parallel.py wraps joblib — its Parallel at L41 subclasses joblib’s own so that configuration and warning filters travel with the task into worker processes, and delayed at L95 is the marker that turns a call into a schedulable unit. The forest code shows the canonical usage: _parallel_build_trees at L135 is the per-tree job, and the BaseForest class at L188 fans it out across processes or threads depending on n_jobs. A subtle detail worth respect: the same module pins thread counts on BLAS libraries during parallel regions, so nested parallelism never thrashes your cores.

Model Selection and Metrics

The selection subsystem is where the estimator contract pays its biggest dividends, because sweeping configurations is only safe if cloning is airtight. The splitters in sklearn/model_selection/_split.py — train_test_split at L2771 for the one-shot case, KFold, L437 for the general rotation — produce index pairs and nothing else — no data, no models — which is why the same splitter objects can be reused across experiments safely.

GridSearchCV in sklearn/model_selection/_search.py then becomes almost simple to read: for every combination of parameters and every fold, clone the base estimator, fit it on the fold’s training slice, and score it on the validation slice. The scoring step is itself pluggable through string names — get_scorer at sklearn/metrics/_scorer.py, L478 resolves "accuracy" or "roc_auc" into a callable, and check_scoring at L947 validates the pairing between estimator and scorer so a regressor is never judged by classification metrics. Underneath, the metrics modules like the one holding accuracy_score at L357 do the actual arithmetic, sharing the same multiclass bookkeeping utilities so results are consistent no matter which entry point you use.

Reading this subsystem end to end changes how you use it. Refitting the best estimator on the full data after the search is not a bolted-on convenience — it falls out of the clone discipline: every fitted candidate is disposable by design, and the search remembers only the winning configuration. That is the kind of property worth copying into your own experiment code.

Honest Limits

For all its polish, scikit-learn is explicit about what it is not. It is not a deep learning framework — there are no GPUs in the core, no autograd, and no batched training of neural networks; that is PyTorch’s territory, and the two cooperate well in mixed workflows. It is not a text or sequence modeling stack; for pretrained language models you will reach for Transformers and treat scikit-learn as the layer around it for classical metrics and calibrations. And it is not a data management system: the bundled datasets are toys and small classics, and anything real belongs in something like Datasets upstream, loaded into NumPy or sparse matrices before fit ever sees it.

Deployment has its own boundary. Fitted scikit-learn models serialize happily with joblib, but serving them outside Python means converting them — the ONNX route is the standard answer, and tools like skl2onnx translate most estimator families to a portable graph that ONNX Runtime executes at native speed. The conversion layer is community-maintained rather than core, so exotic custom estimators are exactly where you should budget testing time.

None of these limits diminish the central achievement. In a field where interfaces churn yearly, one library has kept the same two-verb vocabulary — fit and transform — stable enough that code from a decade ago still runs and reads naturally. Read sklearn/base.py for the contract, sklearn/utils/validation.py for the discipline, and one .pyx kernel for the performance engineering, and you will have absorbed design lessons that outlast any single framework.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of scikit-learn: the fit/transform contract, estimator chaining, Cython kernels, and the model selection machinery, with two architecture diagrams.
